chapter: Fellow musicians: Kirk, Bunk, Parker, McShann
title: Goodwin on Parker's style and hiring him at Lucille's Paradise
summary: Goodwin says Parker blended many players' ideas; he hired him at Lucille's Paradise when no one else would.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Well now Crook, do you agree with that?

Not always, but I'd like to bring out a point. I think what Charlie was doing was creating a style and I don't think the fellows wanted to hear his experiment so much because if you've listened to Charlie play, you will hear a little bit of most any top-notch musician. You'll hear a little Herman Walder and you'll hear a little Buster Smith and you'll hear a little Ben Webster or most any tenor or alto saxophone player within this region at the time.
Well Charlie, he was -- he had big ears. He would listen to all of these guys and he culminated all this together

you know, just got it all together and this is why the guys, I think, didn't want to play with him because they were accustomed to a guy getting up and blowing right on out but Charlie had his style, he was creating, which he had perfected, -- he hadn't perfected.
He had not perfected?
That's right, he had not perfected it and Charlie left here -- when Charlie left here he was playing with a small group that I had. Wouldn't anybody hire Charlie as an alto player.
But you did?
I did.
What room was that?
Lucille's Paradise. 1815 E. 18th St.
Lucille's Paradise. I guess you -- I heard that you were the first band leader to ever hire Charlie, Crook?

Right, right, because he was -- well he was far out. Most people didn't understand him, which I didn't either, but I needed an alto saxophone player and I had Buster Smith -- had the band. He left and went to Dallas, Texas, and I needed an alto saxophone player to fill the engagement and I had a tenor man by the name of West and he was a very good man and I just needed somebody to make seven mix in the pieces, see.
Was Sleepy on that band?
No.
The reason I ask is --
Emil Williams.
Emil Williams, the man that brought Baby up from Shreveport.
Right.

Well Sleepy told me one time, may God rest his soul -- we were traveling on a gig and he told me about Charlie Parker sitting on the sidewalk outside a room where they were playing and crying on Sleepy's shoulder because nobody liked him or thought he was worth anything as an alto man.

That's right, but this wasn't at Lucille's Paradise. Now Charlie played with me I guess about a month and he got itchy feet and he wanted to go to Chicago and he would always come to little Ernie Williams --
The drummer? He worked with Harlan Leonard -- great drummer.

-- he'd always come to Ernie Williams or myself and he would try to get information. 'You fellows have been around, you've been in the game. What must I do here?', and you know, he wanted information about life, not music.
